independence_rule: Facts were established from the local Book VI chapter text before comparison with production JSON or the Book VI production manifest. Canonical IDs are normalization labels only; reader-facing identity knowledge, reported events, intended actions, mistaken beliefs and actual outcomes remain distinct.

chapters.title: A Chat with the Men
functional_actors: young Hosokawa retainers in Tadatoshi's evening circle
historical_context: lance-versus-sword debate in the early Tokugawa peace

facts.description: Tadatoshi uses relaxed evening conversations with young retainers to hear candid opinions and current gossip.
The group debates lance versus sword; Mainosuke repeats Kojirō's argument that sword discipline refines the spirit and has universal military application.
Tadatoshi evaluates Kojirō not only for technical skill but for character and his ability to fit productively into the existing Hosokawa retainer body.
Tadatoshi explicitly compares Kojirō with Musashi, judging Musashi potentially broader in combat and government while recognizing Kojirō's stronger lineage and public reputation.
The retainers read and discuss the anti-Musashi Hangawara notices and largely accept the public image of Musashi as a coward or fraud.
Rather than accept the crowd's judgment, Tadatoshi becomes more interested in hearing Musashi's side of the story.
The next morning Tadatoshi tells Sado to continue looking for Musashi and to bring him in if found.
Tadatoshi separately authorizes Kakubei to bring Kojirō for an interview, keeping both candidates under consideration.

chapters.title: Buzzing Insects
physical_locations: Isarago Hill cemetery and florist area

facts.description: The Drying Pole returns from polishing in unexpectedly excellent condition after the Hōjō Shinzō incident.
Osugi visits Kojirō, gives him her copied Sutra on the Great Love of Parents and discusses the signs attacking Musashi's reputation.
Osugi says she plans to leave Yajibei's household, rent a small place near Yoroi Ferry and continue seeking Matahachi and Musashi independently.
Kakubei tells Kojirō that Tadatoshi is willing to see him and proposes an immediate interview.
Kojirō abruptly withdraws when Kakubei explains that Tadatoshi must inspect him before making a final appointment decision.
The narration reveals that Kojirō's claimed indifference to stipend conceals an enormous ambition for fame, wealth and national recognition.
Yogorō secretly enters Kojirō's quarters at night and attacks the sleeping swordsman in revenge for the destruction of the Obata school.
Kojirō evades the sleeping attack, identifies Yogorō and advances on him with the Drying Pole; the chapter ends before the death is shown directly.

chapters.title: The Eagle
historical_context: Date, Kuroda, Shimazu and Mōri houses
physical_locations: Hosokawa Edo residence and archery range
Okatani Gorōji house near Tokiwa Bridge

facts.description: Kakubei persuades Kojirō to reconsider the interview, and Kojirō agrees to appear before Tadatoshi.
A young samurai corpse lies near the Isarago cemetery; Kojirō privately recognizes it as the youth he cut down, confirming Yogorō's death while the public lacks identification.
Kojirō gives the florist money for flowers and incense for the dead youth while internally justifying the killing.
Kojirō rides the Takanawa highroad to the Hosokawa residence and answers Tadatoshi's questions about lineage, training and the Ganryū style.
Tadatoshi asks for a demonstration and pairs Kojirō with the household's leading lancer, Okatani Gorōji.
Using a wooden sword against Gorōji's real lance, Kojirō breaks the shaft and inflicts severe but nonfatal injury before Tadatoshi stops the bout.
Kojirō later learns that Gorōji survived despite serious injury to the pelvis or thigh.
Kojirō repeatedly visits the wounded Gorōji with cordiality and gifts, explicitly hoping that praise from the defeated man will improve his own public reputation.

chapters.title: Green Persimmons
physical_locations: Donjiki food stall and vacant lot

facts.description: At the Donjiki stall Kojirō hears that the supposedly pious Daizō of Narai has made conspicuous religious donations in Edo.
Hamada and another samurai assault watermelon-vendor Matahachi over a woman he has hidden; Matahachi recognizes Kojirō and calls for help.
Kojirō kills the two attackers and releases Matahachi from their bonds.
Kojirō writes and signs a public statement accepting responsibility for the killings and says he will not flee relatives who seek him.
Matahachi and Akemi are living together and neighbors treat them as a couple, but the narration explicitly states Akemi has not committed to legal marriage and sees the arrangement as temporary.
Umpei, an experienced well-digger boss working for the shōgun's castle project, again offers Matahachi higher-paid work inside the castle grounds.
Akemi reacts with fear when Matahachi says he encountered Kojirō; Matahachi falsely assures her he did not reveal where she lives.
Kojirō secretly follows Matahachi home, observes the couple and finally throws a green persimmon before walking away unseen.

chapters.title: Eyes
functional_actors: laborer hired to help build the cabin

facts.description: Musashi leaves the city atmosphere and anti-Musashi gossip behind, builds a simple cabin on Musashino and plans a period of Zen, reading and sword training with Iori.
Musashi decides Iori must be trained as a samurai for the coming era of order and construction rather than for the vanished age of continuous war.
During wooden-sword practice Musashi repeatedly teaches Iori to hold and understand the opponent's eyes rather than lose mental control under a superior gaze.
After Musashi leaves, Iori practices the lesson by staring down a possum and experiences the encounter as a small breakthrough in courage and concentration.
Shinzō reports that Kagenori has died and that Yogorō also died after going alone to seek revenge on Kojirō.
With Yogorō dead, Shinzō says adoption proceedings arranged through his father and Munenori will make him Kagenori's heir and successor to the Obata name.
Shinzō says Ujikatsu has guests who want to meet Musashi and asks Musashi to return with him to Ushigome.
Unable to guess the hidden guests, Musashi privately hopes Otsū might be among them, mounts Shinzō's horse and leaves Iori at the cabin.

chapters.title: Four Sages with a Single Light
physical_locations: Hōjō residence at Akagi Hill in Ushigome

facts.description: At Ujikatsu's residence Musashi discovers that one surprise guest is Takuan; the old friends exchange news and discuss Musashi's continuing immaturity and training.
Takuan tells Musashi that a young man who claims to understand the Way has stopped growing and that criticism or imperfect reputation can protect genuine development.
Ujikatsu deliberately leads Musashi toward a dark corridor where a hidden swordsman waits to test him; Musashi senses danger and instead circles through the garden.
Musashi infers that the hidden swordsman is Yagyū Munenori from the quality of the presence he sensed and the identities of the other guests.
Munenori greets Musashi as an equal and proposes that the failed ambush test itself be regarded as the bout Musashi had requested.
Munenori tells Musashi that Otsū went to Koyagyū with Hyōgo to help nurse the gravely ill Sekishūsai.
Takuan asks Ujikatsu and Munenori to help reunite Musashi and Otsū; Munenori suggests eventually summoning Otsū and arranging their marriage, but no marriage occurs here.
The three elders agree to recommend Musashi for a position teaching in the shōgun's household despite ancestry and Sekigahara complications.

Musashi internally rejects the sword of conquest and mere technical instruction, defining the Way instead as a means to establish order, protect and refine the spirit and ultimately contribute to peace and good government.
Musashi says he is too immature and still reluctant to marry or settle, but the elders decide to proceed with the recommendation and he does not reject their guardianship.

chapters.title: The Locust Tree
functional_actors: district headman and neighborhood association as administrative gatekeepers

facts.description: Matahachi discovers that Akemi has left their home in good clothes, telling a neighbor she was visiting supposed relatives in Shinagawa.
During an offshore conversation disguised as a fishing trip, Daizō tells Matahachi that he is not really a pawnbroker and offers an enormous payment for a secret mission.
Daizō recruits Matahachi to enter the castle works as one of Umpei's well diggers and shoot Shōgun Hidetada with a hidden musket.
The plan places gun and ammunition beneath the ancient locust tree near the Momiji Hill back gate and calls for Matahachi to escape through the outer moat to accomplices.
After revealing the conspiracy Daizō warns that Matahachi is committed and will be killed within days if he attempts to withdraw.
Matahachi accepts thirty pieces of gold as an advance and confirms that Umpei can bring him into the castle work crew.
Akemi is revealed to be secretly staying with Daizō, enthralled by him after several visits and expecting him to take care of her Matahachi problem.
At Daizō's instruction Akemi follows Matahachi after the payment and watches him bury the gold on Nishikubo Hill.
Daizō immediately digs up the hidden payment and discovers only twenty-eight of the thirty coins, concluding that Matahachi kept two.

chapters.title: Tadaaki’s Madness
historical_context: Mikogami Tenzen renamed Ono Tadaaki after Sekigahara
Ittō Style and shogunal sword instruction

facts.description: Matahachi leaves two gold pieces and a note at Osugi's back door saying he still cannot face her and asking forgiveness for another six months of absence.
Ono-school men searching for Matahachi seize Osugi and use her as a hostage intended to draw their enemies into a confrontation.
Yajibei informs Kojirō that Osugi has vanished and that a message identifies Hamada Toranosuke of the Ono school as her captor.
Kojirō rides the Takanawa highroad to Yajibei's house, questions him in detail and then proceeds the next day through Kanda Hill, Saikachi Slope and Ochanomizu to the Ono residence.
Toranosuke and the Ono students prepare to use Osugi as bait and overwhelm Kojirō with numbers rather than challenge him directly.
Kojirō bypasses the waiting students, goes directly to Tadaaki and holds the teacher responsible for his pupils' misconduct.
In the garden Tadaaki recognizes Kojirō as an extraordinary new-generation fighter and explicitly concedes before either man lands a normal winning strike.
Kojirō attacks immediately after Tadaaki's capitulation and cuts off his topknot; Tadaaki simultaneously slices part of Kojirō's sleeve, provoking outrage among the students.
Tadaaki interprets the defeat as proof that his era has passed, retires from the dōjō to pursue enlightenment and entrusts care of his son Tadanari to Itō Magobei.
Tadaaki condemns complacency in the Ono school and orders the remaining students to make it a training ground capable of developing future talent.
Tadaaki expels Toranosuke for cowardice: delaying direct revenge, pursuing Matahachi, kidnapping Osugi and plotting a group ambush instead of issuing an open challenge.
Tadaaki releases Osugi and allows her to return with Kojirō.
During the aftermath Kojirō learns that Musashi is being considered for a position teaching the shōgun and visibly dislikes the news.
Not many days later Tadaaki leaves Edo to follow his new path, while the public interprets the disappearance as madness after defeat.
A severe typhoon tears the roof from the Musashino cabin and leaves the structure beyond repair despite Iori's precautions.
Musashi spends the aftermath helping neighbors with flood drainage, sickness and cooperative crisis work rather than concentrating on his own ruined house.
Seeing the farmers' gratitude and shared food, Iori learns that forgetting oneself and working for the group can generate reciprocal support.
Iori hears sacred-dance drumming and persuades Musashi to travel to Mitsumine while local farmers rebuild their cabin.
They stay at Tanashi and are later delayed at the swollen Iruma River, where the bridge has been largely destroyed.
Iori finds old weapons and human bones near Kotesashigahara; Musashi makes him gather and bury the remains respectfully.
Musashi connects the bones to the old Kotesashigahara battles and teaches that past warriors' sacrifices form part of the foundation of present peace and prosperity.

Pressed by Iori's questions about loyal and rebel dead, Musashi concludes that a genuine samurai and swordsman must possess compassion and an appreciation of life's poignancy, not merely destructive skill.
At Mitsumine Musashi notices a large donor plaque naming Daizō of Narai and Shibaura Village and decides to investigate.
Temple records show that Daizō has visited several times, but officials refuse or cannot provide useful detail about his identity or companions.
The sacred dances trigger Musashi's memories of childhood festivals and familiar faces from Miyamoto.
Watching a drummer use two sticks to make one sound produces an explicit breakthrough: two swords can function as one coordinated system.
Musashi connects his instinctive two-sword use at Ichijōji with a conscious principle, rejecting custom that treats one-hand use as naturally mandatory.
He defines the desired two-sword method as simultaneously conscious and reflexive, with left and right acting freely like the drummer's two hands.
Musashi tells Iori they will climb to the inner shrine the next morning.

chapters.title: The Demon’s Attendant
historical_context: Mitsumine temple-shrine syncretic complex and treasure house
physical_locations: inner-shrine approach forest and mountain road

facts.description: Okō recognizes Musashi at Mitsumine, tells Baiken and Tōji, and pushes them to use the opportunity for revenge.
Baiken is established as Temma's brother, a former freebooter and Yaegaki chain-ball-sickle master who blames Musashi for the chain of losses following Temma's death.
Baiken mobilizes thirteen attackers for Musashi's inner-shrine route, including lancer priests and freebooters, with Tōji assigned a musket and Baiken his chain-ball-sickle.
During the climb Iori experiences sunrise as Amaterasu, connecting the deity with the maternal bond he feels he lacks.
The ambush begins with a gunshot on the inner-shrine approach; Musashi orders Iori down and immediately fights the surrounding attackers.
Under pressure from multiple attackers Musashi fights with long sword in the right hand and short sword in the left, applying the two-sword principle formed at the festival.
Baiken traps Musashi's long sword with the chain and attacks with the sickle, forcing Musashi to abandon the long weapon and solve the unfamiliar distance problem.
Musashi recognizes the Yaegaki chain's ball and sickle as another two-part weapon system analogous to two swords, which reveals a winning tactical principle.
Musashi closes distance, takes Baiken's sword and kills him with a vertical karatake cut, reacting afterward with compassion rather than triumph.
The previously unrecognized helper is revealed as Gonnosuke, who rescued Iori and struck down the gunman and other attackers from behind.
Afterward they count twelve dead attackers: seven killed by Gonnosuke's staff and five by Musashi's swords.
Okō escapes the scene while Kuro breaks loose and the surviving wounded priest moves away.
Musashi chooses to go down the mountain and report the killings to the local authorities because the violence occurred on shrine territory.
Instead of merely taking his statement, officials bind Musashi and escort him toward town under a force that grows to roughly one hundred guards.
Gonnosuke comforts Iori after Musashi's detention and commits himself to finding a way to free their common teacher.
At the Oinu Teahouse Okō attacks Gonnosuke with a dagger; he disarms her, hurls the dagger through her back and kills her.
A village uproar over the stolen Mitsumine treasure explains why Musashi was arrested as a suspected thief rather than merely questioned about the battle.
At Shōmaru Pass Gonnosuke turns back toward Chichibu to save Musashi while sending Iori toward home.
Iori overhears Daizō and a young companion traveling with deceptive castle-supplier boxes and follows them, suspecting they are the Mitsumine thieves.
At the Kawagoe mound Daizō, Jōtarō and three Kiso confederates add the stolen Mitsumine treasure to a large hidden gold cache and repack it for flight.
Daizō and the Kiso men head down the Kōshū route while Jōtarō is sent back toward Edo to recover the Shibaura cache, burn documents and deal with Akemi.
Iori follows Jōtarō, denounces him as a thief and eventually fights him near the Musashino cabin, using Musashi's eye-training lesson.
The boys discover that both regard Musashi as their teacher; their hostility gives way to shocked recognition even though mistrust remains.
Still struggling in a tree, Iori and Jōtarō fall together and are knocked unconscious.
At Musashi's cabin Takuan recognizes the nearly blind mendicant Aoki Tanzaemon and learns for the first time that Jōtarō is Tanzaemon's son.
Takuan directs the guilt-ridden Tanzaemon to Shōjuan in Edo and promises to help arrange a future meeting with his son.
Takuan and local farmers revive Iori and recognize the older Jōtarō after the boys' fight.
Jōtarō admits helping Daizō rob the treasure house while claiming the theft serves the public; Takuan attacks the logic of a half-educated do-gooder imposing his own idea of social good.
After Takuan reveals that he has just met Jōtarō's father, Jōtarō finally confesses the full secret conspiracy and his promise to Daizō.
Takuan gives Jōtarō money and a Daitokuji seal, orders him to reunite with his father at Shōjuan and travel disguised as priests while avoiding the Kōshū highroad and Nakasendō.
Takuan makes explicit that Daizō's network intends to kill the shōgun, burn Ieyasu's Suruga castle, destabilize Kantō and seize government, making Jōtarō an agent of treason rather than a mere thief.

chapters.title: The Pomegranate
historical_context: Musashi's anti-Tokugawa service at Sekigahara as used in Osugi's accusation

facts.description: Takuan and Iori reach the Hōjō mansion; Takuan continues toward Edo Castle while Iori is left in Shinzō's care.
Osugi appears at the mansion and gives Shinzō a long denunciation of Musashi, citing Sekigahara, alleged crimes and the Otsū dispute to argue he is unfit to teach the shōgun.
Osugi explicitly asks that her accusations be passed to Ujikatsu because she believes he recommended Musashi for the shogunal post.
Furious at the attack on Musashi's name, Iori pelts Osugi with a pomegranate and then horse manure.
Seeing Osugi reduced to tears makes Iori ashamed and torn between pity for her and continued anger over her slander.

chapters.title: Land of Dreams
historical_context: Ieyasu transfers shogunate to Hidetada in 1605
physical_locations: Edo Castle Fukiage and Momiji Hill works

facts.description: Inside the castle works Matahachi repeatedly sees Hidetada but decides he will not carry out the assassination even if that means remaining a well digger.
Matahachi's suspicious wandering around Momiji Hill leads castle work officials to lock him in a woodshed.
Matahachi escapes the shed at night and digs beneath the locust tree to remove the promised musket, but finds only human bone because the weapon has not yet arrived.
Takuan catches Matahachi at the locust tree, returns him to custody and confronts him with the permanence of his own choices rather than allowing him to erase the plot symbolically.
Takuan reveals that Daizō of Narai is really Mizoguchi Shinano, a fugitive retainer tied to the defeated anti-Tokugawa side and now wanted by the shogunate.
Takuan explains that the musket never reached the locust tree because Jōtarō, whom Daizō had drawn into the plot, failed to arrive as planned.
Authorities search Daizō's Kiso base after his escape and discover arms, ammunition and surviving correspondence with Toyotomi supporters.
Musashi is released from prison after the treasure-house misunderstanding is resolved and is formally handed over to Gonnosuke.
Officials confiscate Daizō's Shibaura pawnshop and documents and arrest Akemi even though she knows nothing of the larger treason plot.

Takuan warns Hidetada that obsessively hunting every hidden opponent would consume the effort needed for constructive government; Hidetada orders light punishments and lets Takuan shape the penalties.
Takuan formally asks Hidetada to look favorably on the recommendation of Musashi as a household tutor, and Hidetada indicates willingness to appoint another instructor.
Rather than execution, Matahachi and Akemi are publicly flogged and sentenced to banishment from Edo.
Matahachi realizes with ecstatic relief that he will live and runs off without looking back, while Akemi remains behind recovering from the punishment.
Unable to wait for news, Iori rides away from the Hōjō residence intending to find Musashi in Chichibu and discovers the rebuilt Musashino cabin still empty.
At Nobidome Iori unexpectedly encounters Osugi and a large Hosokawa advance party commanded around Kakubei and including the now formally retained Kojirō.
Kojirō is now a Hosokawa vassal, with altered formal appearance and a substantial stipend, traveling toward Buzen with the advance party.
Osugi is traveling west with the Hosokawa party to restore family affairs in Mimasaka, recover Gonroku's ashes in Osaka and hold neglected memorial services before resuming her vendetta.
The narration reveals that Osugi has systematically denounced Musashi at Yagyū, Hōjō and government households and has thrown written accusations into official compounds to block his appointment.
Kojirō deliberately tests Iori with his gaze; Iori initially holds steady, showing the effect of Musashi's eye training, though Kojirō later overwhelms him when he tries to throw a stone.
Kojirō writes Musashi a sealed letter as Sasaki Ganryū, Retainer to the House of Hosokawa, inviting a future meeting on the boundary between life and death and makes Iori the messenger.
Shaken by Kojirō's strength, Iori resolves that both he and Musashi must grow stronger and decides to continue toward Chichibu with the letter.
On Musashino Plain Iori unexpectedly reunites with Musashi and Gonnosuke, who have found the wandering Hōjō horse near the Iruma River.
Gonnosuke assures Iori that Musashi's innocence in the Mitsumine theft is now established.
Iori gives Kojirō's sealed challenge letter to Musashi and recounts the Nobidome encounter.
The three spend the night together in the rebuilt Musashino cabin, restoring the teacher-disciple household temporarily.

chapters.title: The Gateway to Glory
historical_context: Eastern-versus-Western alignment before final Edo-Osaka conflict
Chinese and Japanese painting traditions influencing Musashi

facts.description: Five former Obata students tell Shinzō they believe Kojirō killed Yogorō and propose pursuing the new Hosokawa vassal west to take revenge.
Shinzō refuses an immediate group attack, openly admitting Kojirō is the better swordsman and arguing that rushing him with numbers would only deepen the school's disgrace.
Shinzō tells Iori that Musashi is expected to become one of the shōgun's teachers and founder of his own sword school.
The Council of Elders summons Musashi to the Reception Pavilion outside Wadakura Gate for confirmation before an audience with the shōgun.
Musashi privately wants to refuse because he fears official status will abort his pursuit of the Way, but accepts out of loyalty to the friends who placed their trust in him.
After Musashi waits nearly half a day, Sakai Tadakatsu apologetically tells him that the shōgun reversed the expected appointment and that the Council of Elders could not change the decision.
Musashi genuinely receives the cancellation with gratitude, feeling that a higher path has opened outside official glory.
Tadakatsu suggests that instead of answering malicious gossip verbally, Musashi leave a wordless artistic testimony to the purity of his character.
Musashi paints Musashino Plain with a great vermilion rising sun symbolizing confidence in his own integrity, then leaves without looking back.
At the gate Musashi explicitly wonders whether true glory lies inside or outside the castle, completing the chapter's reversal of expected success.

chapters.title: The Sound of Heaven
functional_actors: official who reports the adverse appointment file
historical_context: military and literary arts as complementary bases of government
Minamoto no Sanetomo poem in San'emon's testament
referenced_locations: central-provinces temple where Iori's sister was abandoned

facts.description: Musashi returns to the Musashino cabin in formal clothes and tells Gonnosuke the appointment was canceled, adding that he considers the outcome fortunate.

Musashi says the Way of the Sword and good government should ultimately align, but he now sees that governance requires a perfect blending of military and literary arts and that he still has much to learn from the country itself.
Musashi decides to leave for the mountains and continue training rather than remain near Edo seeking an official appointment.
Musashi asks Gonnosuke to look after Iori for the next two or three years and returns to the boy the keepsake pouch left by his father.
Musashi avoids returning personally to Ujikatsu because he fears closer association with a man rejected as suspicious could create political trouble for his patron.
At the Hōjō residence an official report and Shinzō's account establish that adverse stories about Musashi, especially Osugi's long vendetta and accusations, materially damaged the appointment.
Musashi's short letter contains no bitterness and says he is yielding to wanderlust and leaving the Floating World for another aimless journey.
Takuan reads the crumpled message in Iori's inherited pouch and learns that San'emon and his wife once abandoned a daughter at a temple in the central provinces.

The testament says the abandoned daughter was left with the phrase 'one sound of heaven'; Takuan recognizes the clue as Otsū's flute and realizes he knows Iori's lost sister, without yet explaining the identity to Iori.
The group rushes to the Musashino cabin hoping to see Musashi before he leaves, but arrives at dawn to find the house empty.
